The files hold the tool definitions each server served, every recorded change field by field, pattern scan matches, and advisory classifier readings. A signed manifest lists checksums so users can verify files, and the data is released under CC BY 4.0. ## What it does The site says HISTOR reads the tool list of every remote server in the official MCP registry each day and runs each new npm and PyPI MCP package version in a sandbox. It presents its pattern matches and classifier flags as leads worth reading, not as proof that a server is malicious. ### Stated on the product site License CC BY 4.0 Release cadence A full snapshot published as files once a month Verification A manifest of file checksums, signed with Ed25519 Mirrors Hugging Face with one tag per snapshot, Zenodo with a DOI per snapshot Coverage limit Servers that require a key show less or nothing to the anonymous client Code link The page links a GitHub repository for the project ### Not stated on the site * The page does not name the LLM behind the advisory classifier readings. * The page does not say what the sandbox run of a package records beyond its tool list. * How server operators' opt-out requests are handled beyond opening an issue is not described on the page. Issues · Pull requests HISTOR (ἵστωρ, “the one who knows because they saw”) — a public transparency log of MCP tool definitions What every remote MCP endpoint in the official registry advertised · when it changed · signed, appended, auditable English · Русский · Español · Français · 中文 > WARDEN quality cycle: MOMUS → AI-Factory → SKOPOS → shared node agent → deployment. Live: histor.modelmarket.dev · Landing: alexar76.github.io/histor · Capabilities: `histor.check@v1` · `histor.server@v1` · `histor.changes@v1` · Port: `9490` ## The problem, in one paragraph An MCP server can pass your review with harmless tool descriptions and change them later — a new sentence in a description is all a prompt injection needs, and your client will pass it to the model without asking you again. MCP has no content addressing for tool definitions, the official registry verifies namespaces rather than contents, and a scanner on your laptop sees only what the server shows your laptop. HISTOR is the missing public memory: it records what each server advertised, signs it, and tells anyone who asks whether what they received is what everyone else is seeing. ## What it does `flowchart LR R["Official MCP registry
~21k servers"] --> C["Crawler
server/discover + tools/list
never a tool call"] C --> D["MTL/1 digest
RFC 8785 + SHA-256"] D --> L["Four signed labels
AWR/2 · did:key"] W["WARDEN sidecar
published pattern set"] --> L L --> M["Merkle log
RFC 9162"] M --> S["Signed tree head
after every crawl"] M --> API["Desk · API · badge · Atom feed"] CL["Your client"] -- "tools it received" --> K["/api/v1/check"] K -- "signed: same · different · seen before" --> CL K -. "opt-in digest count" .-> M ` * Reads every remote endpoint in the official registry: `server/discover`, then `tools/list` (legacy servers use initialization) drained across pages. No tool is called, nothing is installed or executed, private addresses are refused before a connection opens. * Also reads a short list of popular remote servers the registry does not carry (`histor/curated.json`, DeepWiki among them), under HISTOR's own namespace `urn:awr:mtl:1:registry:histor.modelmarket.dev/curated`, so no label claims a registry listing. When such a server publishes to the registry, the registry's listing replaces ours. * Runs npm and PyPI packages — the servers people start locally with `npx` or `uvx` — in a sandbox: installed without running their code, started under gVisor with decoy credentials and no route out, read with discovery and `tools/list` (legacy initialization when needed), then up to 15 tools called once with canary arguments, inside the sandbox. gVisor's own trace says what the package did — programs started, names looked up, decoys opened — at install, at startup and when its tools were called. Completed observations are cached per published version; incomplete observations are retried; a new version that changes what its tools tell the model is a change in the log, like any endpoint's. * Digests the tool set exactly as MTL/1 defines it — name, description, input and output schema, UTF-16 code-unit order, RFC 8785. * Signs four kinds of label, each a standalone AWR/2 `VerificationVerdict`: what was observed, what the WARDEN pattern set matched, whether the definitions changed since the previous label, and whether the name is on a threat list. * Appends every label to an RFC 9162 Merkle log and signs a tree head after each crawl, so a consistency proof shows the history was only ever appended to. * Answers `/check`: send the tools your client received; get back, signed, whether HISTOR observed the same set at that endpoint, an earlier one, or none. Remote checks run independently of the daily registry/package cycle. The default target interval is six hours; endpoints with at least two observed changes in the last seven days are checked every 30 minutes. These are scheduling targets: host limits, failures and queue capacity can make actual gaps longer. Intermediate states can still be missed. See remote polling operations for configuration and measured intervals. Release changes and upgrade notes: CHANGELOG.md. MCP 2026-07-28: modern and legacy compatibility. Local upgrade brief: choose your dependencies and workflows, compare saved observations, and get a retest checklist. From this source directory, run `python3 -m histor upgrade-brief --watchlist examples/upgrade-brief/watchlist.json --out-dir ../output/histor-upgrade-brief-example/en` (Python 3.11+). Reports and checklists support `--lang ru|en|es|fr|zh` (default `en`). See the guide and reproducible synthetic example, available in five languages. ## What a label does not say The profile forbids the words safe, secure, audited, certified, approved and trusted, and so does this README. A pattern match is a reason to read a definition, not a finding. Three of the four methods can never return `fail`; the fourth (continuity) fails only in the mechanical sense that two digests differ. No source is read, no package resolved, no behaviour observed. A change is shown as a date and a diff, never as an accusation. Details: docs/labels.md. What a tool list costs. A client resends every connected server's tool list with each model request. Over the 18,204 packages and 16,170 remote servers in the log, a list's median is about 1,300 tokens, the 90th percentile about 8,000, and 31 packages list over 100,000: docs/tool-list-cost.md. Each count is split into names, descriptions and input schemas; every change carries its cost diff (`/api/v1/changes//cost`), and `histor tool-cost check` runs the same count in a package's CI and fails a release that makes the list heavier: docs/tool-list-cost.md. Download the data. Once a week the log's whole view is published as files at histor.modelmarket.dev/datasets/: every listed server, every tool set it showed, every recorded change and the WARDEN scans. The files are JSON Lines (gzip) with a manifest signed by the log's key; the compilation is CC BY 4.0. Each snapshot's README lists the fields and loads in pandas or DuckDB (histor/dataset.py). Also on Hugging Face; to cite: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23512759. Public payer evidence. The `histor payer-audit` command (since 0.4.1) checks Base USDC receipts and exports sourced behavioural indications while retaining payment totals and unknown cases.
